opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I've heard that reaction a fair amount, and honestly I think it's a pretty natural one. There are really two flavors of it, and I'd respond to them a bit differently.

The first flavor is something like, "Of course the model plans ahead when it writes a rhyming poem," or "Of course it does multi-step reasoning, it gets the answer right, so it must be doing something like that." And I get it, if you look at the behavior, you can form a hypothesis about what's going on inside. But a hypothesis from behavior isn't the same as seeing the mechanism. For a long time, a very reasonable position was that these models are just doing next-token prediction in a fairly shallow way: they pick up surface statistics, and when they look like they're planning or reasoning, that's an illusion created by pattern matching over a huge training set. Plenty of smart people held that view, and you couldn't really rule it out by just looking at outputs. So when we look inside and see that, on the line before a rhyme, the model has already activated features for candidate rhyming words, and that those features actually shape how it constructs the line, that's evidence, not intuition. And when we intervene, suppress that planned word or inject a different one, the model rewrites the line to land on the new target. That's the part that moves it from "seems obvious" to "we actually know this."

The second flavor is more like, "Well, I already believed that." And to that, I'd say: great! Plenty of results in science confirm what some people already suspected. That's still really valuable, because different people had different, often contradictory, intuitions, and some of them were wrong. If you'd polled people beforehand on whether the model computes addition with a lookup table, the algorithm you learned in school, or something else, you'd have gotten a spread of answers. What we found was this kind of parallel-pathways thing, one path doing rough magnitude estimation and another nailing the last digit, which isn't what most people would have guessed, and the model, when asked, describes the schoolbook carry-the-one algorithm instead of what it actually does. That gap between what the model says it's doing and what it's actually doing is not obvious at all, and it matters a lot for questions like whether we can trust chain-of-thought explanations.

And the last thing I'd add is that the point of the work isn't only the individual findings. It's that we now have a method, these attribution graphs on top of a replacement model, that lets you go into a model and ask, for a specific prompt, "what's the mechanism here?" and get a partial, testable answer. Even if a given finding matches your intuition, being able to check intuitions is the thing that's been missing. Sometimes the check confirms you, sometimes it surprises you, as with hallucinations, where the default seems to be "I can't answer" and a "known entity" feature inhibits that default, which gives you a pretty concrete story for how hallucinations happen when that inhibition misfires. Having a microscope is useful precisely because you don't know in advance which of your intuitions will survive.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts the reaction that findings were obvious with the range of differing prior intuitions, noting that the addition mechanism was not what most people would have guessed and that some intuitions were wrong.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think that reaction is really interesting, and honestly I think it's a little bit of a mixed thing. On one hand, I take it as a kind of compliment, right? If you read the paper and your reaction is "well, of course the model does that," I think that means the explanation we gave is actually legible, it makes sense, it fits with your intuitions about how these things should work. That's kind of what you want from an explanation.

But I'd push back on it a little bit, because I think there's a big difference between something being plausible in hindsight and something being obvious in advance. If you'd asked people before we did this work, "how does the model add two numbers?" or "how does it plan a rhyme in a poem?" you'd have gotten a bunch of different answers, and a lot of them would have been wrong. Like, the planning result in poetry — the idea that the model picks the rhyming word ahead of time and then writes the line to get there — plenty of people, including people at Anthropic, kind of assumed these models were just doing something much more myopic, token by token. And for addition, people had very different theories, some of them that it's just memorized a giant lookup table, some that it's doing something like the algorithm we learned in school. And what we found doesn't look like either of those; it's this sort of parallel thing with rough magnitude estimates and precise low-digit features that get combined. Nobody that I know of predicted that in detail.

The other thing I'd say is that the goal of the paper wasn't really to produce surprising facts. The goal was to show that we can actually look, that we have a method where you can go in and trace what the model is doing on a specific prompt and get an answer that's grounded in the mechanics rather than in a story we tell ourselves. And some of the results confirmed intuitions, some of them didn't, and I think both are valuable. The cases where the model's stated reasoning doesn't match what's actually going on inside, the unfaithful chain-of-thought stuff, those are cases where the "obvious" story is actually wrong, and you only find that out by looking.

So I guess my view is, if it feels obvious, great, that means it's understandable. But I'd be careful about trusting that feeling too much, because I think a lot of the things people call obvious after the fact are things they would have gotten wrong if you'd made them bet beforehand.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes findings that seem obvious in hindsight from findings people would have predicted beforehand, noting that many would have guessed incorrectly before the work.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a distinction between something being plausible and actually having evidence for it. You can look at a model’s behavior and come up with a story about how it works, but there might be several different mechanisms that would produce that same behavior.

So when someone says, “Of course the model does that,” the question is: Could we have predicted that beforehand? And can we test it? If we think we’ve identified a mechanism, can we intervene on it and change the model’s behavior in the way we expect? That’s a much stronger claim than saying the explanation sounds reasonable.

Some findings may confirm intuitions people already had, and that’s useful. The point is to move from a plausible story to something we can investigate and test.

r001.rationale: The response discusses claims that findings are obvious and asks whether they could have been predicted beforehand, but it does not observe that findings can seem obvious after publication despite having been surprising before publication.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a difference between having an intuition about what a model might be doing and actually finding evidence for it. You might expect a model to represent related concepts in related ways. But that doesn’t tell you where those representations are, how to identify them, or whether changing them will change the model’s behavior in the way you predict.

So I’m sympathetic to the reaction that some of the findings feel intuitive. That’s encouraging. But the interesting part is turning that intuition into something you can test. And then you have to be careful about what you’ve established: finding an interpretable feature is progress, but it’s still a long way from understanding the full computation the model is performing.

r001.rationale: The response says some findings feel intuitive and distinguishes intuition from evidence, but it does not say they were surprising before publication and seemed obvious afterward.
